name: message-filter
intent: Put a criterion between a channel and its consumers so that only the messages matching it are forwarded and every other message is discarded before a consumer ever sees it.
problem: A channel carries far more traffic than a particular consumer wants or is allowed to see - price updates for instruments it does not trade, telemetry from sites it does not operate, events from tenants it must not touch - and without a gate every consumer has to receive, deserialise and re-check the same messages, wasting capacity and widening the data it touches.
context: Message-based integration over point-to-point queues or publish-subscribe feeds where the receiver's interest is expressible as a predicate over headers, routing keys or the body; where dropping the rest is acceptable, or an Invalid Message Channel / Dead Letter Channel collects the rejects; and where the criterion is stable enough to be configured once - as a broker subscription rule, a message selector, a routing-key binding or a predicate in the stream pipeline.
benefits: Consumers see only their slice: fewer messages to receive, deserialise, store and protect, so both processing cost and the data-exposure surface shrink.
Interest is expressed once - as a predicate, subscription rule, selector or routing-key binding - instead of being re-checked by every handler on the channel.
Rejects are cheap and happen as early as the platform allows: a broker-side filter drops messages before delivery, an edge filter drops them before deserialisation.

Filters compose: they chain into pipelines, combine with a Publish-Subscribe Channel so each subscriber keeps its own slice of one feed, and can be re-pointed at a discard channel when rejects must be preserved.
Producers and consumers stay decoupled: publishers keep emitting one feed while each consumer declares its own interest at the boundary instead of asking the producer to split topics.
tradeoffs: Discards are silent and permanent: a Message Filter has a single output channel, so a non-matching message is gone. Preserving it takes an explicit Invalid Message Channel / Dead Letter Channel - and with two outputs the component is a Content-Based Router, with another path to operate and monitor.

An over-strict criterion starves a consumer without raising an error: the symptom is reduced traffic, not a failure, so counting and alerting on filtered messages is part of the pattern rather than an optional extra.

Body-based criteria force you to pay for the decision: the message must be received and usually parsed first, whereas header/routing-key criteria are cheap; broker-side expression filters (SQL-like rules) measurably lower throughput.

The criterion moves out of the code path it guards: broker rules, selectors and binding keys are configuration deployed and reviewed separately from the consumer, so a filter fault is a config change nobody reviewed with the code.
It is a routing convenience, not a security boundary: tenant isolation implemented as a predicate over a shared channel fails open - a wrong criterion leaks data instead of denying access.
Every criterion duplicates knowledge of the message schema (property names, value domains), so schema evolution breaks filters silently, in the code copies and in the configuration copies alike.

participants.responsibility: Evaluates the criterion for every incoming message and forwards only the accepted ones; messages that fail are discarded - or handed to the discard channel - and never reach the output.
The predicate, rule or selector that defines interest (header or property comparison, routing-key pattern, body predicate); best carried as data so interest can change without redeploying consumers.
The feed being filtered - a queue or a publish-subscribe channel; the filter consumes from it and must settle or acknowledge rejected messages where the transport requires it.
Carries only accepted messages; its consumers may rely on the criterion already having been applied (the slice contract).
Collects rejected messages for diagnosis, audit or replay when silent drops are unacceptable; adding it turns the component into a two-output router and needs its own retention policy.

use_cases: A price or promotion feed where each customer subscribes only to the items it trades, so interest is declared per subscriber instead of per topic.
Tenant or site isolation on a shared event stream: an analytics consumer receives only its own tenant's telemetry, with channel-level ACLs as the real enforcement.
Noise suppression ahead of an expensive stage: dropping heartbeats, debug-level events or duplicate notifications before parsing, enrichment or storage.
Routing a shared bus to per-domain handlers on a routing key or correlation id - Camel's `.filter(simple(...))`, a JMS consumer's message selector, an Azure Service Bus subscription rule.
In-process stream processing: a predicate guard in a consumer loop or iterator pipeline that skips messages the current worker cannot handle (unsupported version, stale timestamp, poison marker).
An Apache Camel route uses the Filter EIP predicate to send only matching exchanges through its child endpoints, with the optional status property exposing whether each exchange matched.

An Azure Service Bus topic subscription uses correlation or SQL filters over system and user properties so each subscription receives only its declared slice; correlation filters are preferred when equality matching is sufficient.
A Kafka Streams KStream applies its filter predicate to create a downstream stream containing only records that satisfy the predicate, keeping the filtering step in the stream topology.
avoid_when: Every message must still reach the consumer and it merely ignores some of them: no component is needed - a guarded `continue` in the handler suffices.

Rejected messages must be preserved: use an Invalid Message Channel or Dead Letter Channel directly; if the rejects have consumers of their own, model that explicitly as a Content-Based Router with two outputs.
The decision needs fields the message does not carry yet, or the receiver wants only some fields of each message: enrich first (Content Enricher) or trim the payload (Content Filter), then filter.
The transport already supports the criterion declaratively (topic subscription, routing-key binding, message selector): configure the channel instead of duplicating it in consumer code.
Interest depends on position, request context or runtime state: a Dynamic Router or Routing Slip expresses 'skip the next three' and per-request rules; a static filter cannot.
Messages must be acknowledged and recorded for audit even when the consumer is uninterested: keep delivery and record the decision (Wire Tap, Message History) rather than dropping.
anti_patterns: Security boundary: tenant or role isolation implemented only as a filter predicate on a shared channel, so a rule mistake leaks data instead of denying access (separate channels plus ACLs are the control; the filter is an optimisation on top).
Invisible drop: no counter, no log, no discard channel - when the criterion becomes too strict the consumer simply stops receiving and nobody notices.
Filter-as-parser: deserialising every message just to decide interest that was already available in a header or routing key, paying full cost for traffic that is discarded.
Rule-engine creep: the predicate grows into dozens of imperative branches and per-tenant special cases instead of a declarative rule set or a Content-Based Router.
Duplicate criteria: the same rule copied into several consumers, or into consumer code and broker configuration, so the copies drift apart and disagree about what is interesting.
design_principles: Single responsibility: the filter decides interest and nothing else - no transformation, no enrichment, no retry.
Separation of policy from mechanism: the criterion is data (rule, selector, predicate value), the channel plumbing is mechanism, so new interest does not change transport code (open/closed).
Fail fast and cheap: decide as early as possible - at the broker, at the edge, before parsing - and never transport what you are going to discard.
Data minimisation: a consumer should see only the slice it needs; that is a security and cost property, not merely a performance one.
Rejection is a decision and must be observable: counters, logs or a discard channel - silence is this pattern's characteristic failure mode.
best_practices: Prefer header, metadata or routing-key criteria; inspect the body only when the contract makes it unavoidable, and account for the parsing cost per message.
Push the criterion onto the platform when it can express it declaratively - subscription rules, message selectors, routing-key bindings - so non-matching traffic never leaves the broker.
Keep the predicate pure and unit-test it at the boundaries: missing header, malformed body, empty payload and the exact values that flip the decision.
Make rejects observable: count them (or record a match status), and alert when the accepted/rejected ratio shifts unexpectedly.
Use an Invalid Message Channel or Dead Letter Channel whenever rejects have diagnostic or audit value; never rely on 'we can replay from the beginning'.
Settle or acknowledge dropped messages explicitly (complete, ack, commit) - an unsettled message stays locked or is redelivered forever.
Version criteria like code: a rule or selector change is a behaviour change, so review, test and roll it out deliberately.
sources: Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns: Designing, Building, and Deploying Messaging Solutions (2003) - Message Filter (Message Routing chapter).
